title: Information Theory and Inference
text:
0.1 Scope
These are lecture notes for Information Theory and Inference (third-semester elective, Master in Physics of Data, University of Padova, instructor Prof. Michele Allegra). The course starts from Shannon’s operational definition of information and ends with modern Markov-Chain Monte Carlo methods for high-dimensional Bayesian inference.
The two halves of the course share a single organising object: the probability distribution. In Part I we ask how much information such a distribution contains, and how many bits are needed to communicate outcomes over a noisy channel. In Part II we ask, given a small amount of data, how to sample from a posterior distribution we can evaluate only up to an unknown normalisation constant.

title: Information Theory and Inference
text:
0.2 Reading the notes
Chapters 1–5 build up Shannon’s toolbox: surprisal, entropy, KL divergence, mutual information, and the two coding theorems (source and noisy-channel). Chapters 6–8 pivot to time series and computational statistics: Markov chains, MCMC, Metropolis and Gibbs sampling, with a high-dimensional inference example illustrating how the tools fit together.
Every chapter uses the styled callout environments (definition, theorem, proposition, lemma, corollary, example, remark, note, exercise, solution) so that key results can be scanned without reading the surrounding prose.

title: Information Theory and Inference
text:
0.3 Notation

\(X, Y, Z\): random variables; \(x, y, z\) realisations; \(\mathcal X\) their alphabet.
\(p_X(x) = P(X = x)\), \(p(x, y)\): probability mass or density; \(p(x \mid y)\) conditional.
\(H(X)\), \(H(X, Y)\), \(H(X \mid Y)\): entropy, joint entropy, conditional entropy.
\(I(X; Y)\): mutual information; \(D(p \| q)\): Kullback–Leibler divergence.
\(C\): channel capacity; \(R\): code rate.
\(\pi(\mathbf x)\): target distribution in MCMC; \(T(\mathbf x \to \mathbf x')\): transition kernel; \(q(\mathbf x' \mid \mathbf x)\): proposal.

title: 2  Defining information
text:
2.1 Events and probability spaces
Information theory begins with a puzzle: what does it mean, quantitatively, that one message is more informative than another? Shannon’s answer — that the information content of an event is the logarithm of the reciprocal of its probability — turns out to have a striking number of good properties. This chapter fixes the vocabulary and derives the first quantity of interest, the entropy of a probability space.
We assume the reader is familiar with probability. Recall the standard structure:
For most of what follows we work with a finite alphabet \(\mathcal X\) and take \(\Omega = \mathcal X\), \(\mathcal F = 2^{\mathcal X}\). The atomic events are singletons \(\{x\}\) with probabilities \(p_X(x) = P(\{X = x\})\).

title: 2  Defining information
text: A probability space is a triple \((\Omega, \mathcal F, P)\) where \(\Omega\) is the sample space, \(\mathcal F\) a \(\sigma\)-algebra of events (subsets of \(\Omega\)), and \(P : \mathcal F \to [0, 1]\) a probability measure obeying the Kolmogorov axioms.

title: 2  Defining information
text:
2.2 The surprisal
The right quantitative notion of “how much information does the event \(\{X = x\}\) carry” turns out to be the surprisal.

The surprisal (or self-information) of an event \(A\) with probability \(P(A)\) is \[I(A) = -\log_2 P(A) \quad \text{bits}.\] For a random variable \(X\) taking value \(x\) we write \(I(x) = -\log_2 p_X(x)\).


The function \(I(A) = f(P(A))\) is uniquely determined (up to the choice of logarithm base) by three properties:

Monotonicity. \(I\) is a decreasing function of \(P\): rarer events are more surprising.
Non-negativity. \(I \geq 0\), with \(I = 0\) iff \(P = 1\).
Additivity for independent events. If \(A, B\) are independent, \(I(A \cap B) = I(A) + I(B)\).

Cauchy’s functional equation forces \(f(p) = -\log_c p\) for some base \(c > 1\); the choice \(c = 2\) measures information in bits.


Remark. The base of the logarithm is a matter of units, not physics. \(c = 2\) gives bits (Shannon), \(c = e\) gives nats (Kolmogorov), \(c = 10\) gives dits/hartleys. All results in the notes can be rewritten in any base by multiplying entropy by the appropriate constant.


For a fair coin, \(p(H) = p(T) = 1/2\): each outcome carries \(\log_2 2 = 1\) bit of information. For a biased coin with \(p(H) = 0.99\), seeing heads carries only \(-\log_2 0.99 \approx 0.014\) bits — the outcome was almost certain. Seeing tails carries \(-\log_2 0.01 \approx 6.6\) bits — a much more informative event.

title: 2  Defining information
text:
2.3 Probability trees
A useful visualisation for compound events is the probability tree: a rooted tree with edges labelled by conditional probabilities, whose leaves are the possible outcomes. Multiplying probabilities along a path gives the probability of the corresponding sequence.

For any sequence of events \(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n\), \[I(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} I(x_i \mid x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1}),\] where \(I(x_i \mid \cdot) = -\log_2 p(x_i \mid \cdot)\) is the conditional surprisal.

This is a direct consequence of the chain rule \(p(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = \prod_i p(x_i \mid x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1})\) and additivity of the logarithm.

title: 2  Defining information
text:
2.4 Information for a probability space
The surprisal is the information of a single outcome. To characterise the information content of the whole distribution, we average over all outcomes.

The Shannon entropy of a discrete random variable \(X\) with distribution \(p_X\) is \[H(X) = -\sum_{x \in \mathcal X} p_X(x)\,\log_2 p_X(x) = \mathbb E[I(X)] .\] By convention \(0\log 0 = 0\).

The entropy is the expected number of bits of information carried by a random outcome. This is Shannon’s operational reading, and it will be justified rigorously by the source-coding theorem in Chapter 3.

For \(X \sim \text{Bern}(p)\), \(H(X) = -p\log_2 p - (1-p)\log_2(1-p) \equiv h_2(p)\). The binary entropy function \(h_2\) is symmetric around \(p = 1/2\), where it takes its maximum value \(h_2(1/2) = 1\) bit. It vanishes at \(p = 0\) or \(p = 1\) — no information from a certain outcome.


For a variable \(X\) taking \(M\) values, the entropy is maximised when \(p_X\) is uniform, in which case \(H(X) = \log_2 M\). Non-uniform distributions give strictly less entropy — a preview of the general theorem that entropy is concave in \(p\).

title: 2  Defining information
text:
2.5 Elementary properties
The entropy is well-behaved as a function of the distribution.

For any discrete random variable \(X\) with distribution on \(\mathcal X\):

\(H(X) \geq 0\), with equality iff \(X\) is deterministic.
\(H(X) \leq \log_2 |\mathcal X|\), with equality iff \(X\) is uniform.
\(H\) is a concave function of \(p_X\).
Grouping property. If two outcomes \(x_1, x_2\) are merged into one with probability \(p_1 + p_2\), then \[H(X) = H(X_{merged}) + (p_1 + p_2)\,h_2\bigl(p_1/(p_1 + p_2)\bigr).\]



For a pair \((X, Y)\) with joint distribution \(p(x, y)\), \[H(X, Y) = -\sum_{x, y} p(x, y)\log_2 p(x, y) \leq H(X) + H(Y),\] with equality iff \(X, Y\) are independent (this is a special case of the sub-additivity property proved in Chapter 2).

title: 2  Defining information
text:
2.6 Exercises

A fair die is rolled. Compute (i) the surprisal of the event “the outcome is 6”, (ii) the entropy of the rolling process, (iii) the surprisal of the event “the outcome is even”.


Solution. 

\(I(\{6\}) = -\log_2(1/6) = \log_2 6 \approx 2.585\) bits.
\(H(X) = \log_2 6 \approx 2.585\) bits (uniform on 6 outcomes).
\(I(\{2, 4, 6\}) = -\log_2(3/6) = 1\) bit — exactly one bit of information (equivalent to a coin toss).



Show that for a Bernoulli\((p)\) variable the entropy is maximised at \(p = 1/2\) by direct differentiation. What is the second derivative at the maximum?


Solution. \(H'(p) = -\log_2 p + \log_2(1 - p) = \log_2\bigl((1-p)/p\bigr)\). Setting \(H' = 0\) gives \(p = 1/2\). The second derivative is \(H''(p) = -[1/(p\ln 2) + 1/((1 - p)\ln 2)]\), which at \(p = 1/2\) equals \(-4/\ln 2 \approx -5.77\). Negative \(H''\) confirms concavity — a global maximum.


Verify the grouping property for a three-outcome variable with probabilities \((1/2, 1/4, 1/4)\).


Solution. Direct: \(H = -\tfrac12\log_2\tfrac12 - \tfrac14\log_2\tfrac14 - \tfrac14\log_2\tfrac14 = 1.5\) bits. Grouping the last two into a merged outcome of probability \(1/2\): \(H_{merged} = h_2(1/2) = 1\) bit, plus \(1/2 \cdot h_2(1/2) = 0.5\) bits, total \(1.5\) bits. ✓

title: 2  Defining information
text:
2.7 Callouts






Shannon’s definition is operational — it derives its meaning from the coding theorems of Chapter 3. Purely axiomatic derivations (e.g. Khinchin’s) are elegant but do not tell you why the answer is useful.









When computing entropies by hand, remember the identity \(\log_2 n = \log_2 e \cdot \ln n \approx 1.4427 \ln n\): it lets you convert between nats and bits without a calculator.









The convention \(0\log 0 = 0\) is genuine, not a hack: \(p \log(1/p) \to 0\) as \(p \to 0^+\). But if you compute \(I(x)\) for an event that has empirical probability zero from a finite sample, the value is \(+\infty\), and downstream computations will be nonsense. Always regularise.

title: 3  Information-theoretic measures
text:
3.1 Properties of Shannon entropy
Entropy is only the first in a family of information measures. This chapter introduces the three most useful ones — conditional entropy, mutual information, and KL divergence — and develops the identities and inequalities that connect them. Every result here will be used in the coding theorems of Chapters 3–4.
We first collect a few properties beyond the elementary ones of Chapter 1.
The log-sum inequality is the workhorse behind almost every information-theoretic inequality that follows.

title: 3  Information-theoretic measures
text:
The Shannon entropy \(H : \Delta_M \to [0, \log M]\) on the probability simplex is a strictly concave function of \(p\): for any two distributions \(p, q\) and \(\lambda \in [0, 1]\), \[H(\lambda p + (1 - \lambda)q) \geq \lambda H(p) + (1 - \lambda)H(q),\] with equality iff \(p = q\).


For non-negative reals \(a_i, b_i > 0\), \[\sum_i a_i \log \frac{a_i}{b_i} \geq \Bigl(\sum_i a_i\Bigr)\log \frac{\sum_i a_i}{\sum_i b_i},\] with equality iff \(a_i / b_i\) is constant across \(i\).

title: 3  Information-theoretic measures
text:
3.2 Kullback–Leibler divergence
The KL divergence measures how far one distribution \(p\) is from another \(q\).

For distributions \(p, q\) on a discrete alphabet \(\mathcal X\), \[D(p \| q) = \sum_{x \in \mathcal X} p(x) \log_2 \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}.\] By convention \(0\log(0/q) = 0\) and \(p\log(p/0) = +\infty\) for \(p > 0\).


For any two distributions \(p, q\) on the same alphabet, \(D(p \| q) \geq 0\), with equality iff \(p = q\).

Proof idea. Apply Jensen’s inequality to the convex function \(-\log\) with expectation over \(p\): \(-\log \mathbb E_p[q/p] \leq \mathbb E_p[-\log(q/p)]\); the left-hand side vanishes because \(\mathbb E_p[q(X)/p(X)] = \sum_x q(x) = 1\), so the right-hand side is non-negative.

Remark. The KL divergence is not a metric: it is not symmetric (\(D(p \| q) \neq D(q \| p)\) in general) and does not satisfy the triangle inequality. It nonetheless functions as a “distance” in the sense that \(D(p \| q) = 0 \iff p = q\), and it is convex in each argument.


For \(p \sim \text{Bern}(p_1)\) and \(q \sim \text{Bern}(p_2)\), \[D(p \| q) = p_1 \log_2 \frac{p_1}{p_2} + (1 - p_1)\log_2\frac{1 - p_1}{1 - p_2}.\] When \(p_2 = 1/2\) this reduces to \(1 - h_2(p_1)\), the “distance from uniform” of a biased coin.

title: 3  Information-theoretic measures
section: 3.3 Joint entropy, mutual information, conditional entropy
text:
3.3 Joint entropy, mutual information, conditional entropy
Given two random variables \(X, Y\) we can build several information quantities from their joint distribution.

\[H(X, Y) = -\sum_{x, y} p(x, y) \log_2 p(x, y), \qquad H(Y \mid X) = \sum_x p(x)\,H(Y \mid X = x) .\] The conditional entropy \(H(Y \mid X)\) is the average uncertainty remaining in \(Y\) once \(X\) is known.


\[H(X, Y) = H(X) + H(Y \mid X) = H(Y) + H(X \mid Y).\] More generally, \(H(X_1, \ldots, X_n) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} H(X_i \mid X_1, \ldots, X_{i-1})\).

The chain rule generalises the corresponding rule for surprisal in Chapter 1.

The mutual information between \(X\) and \(Y\) is \[I(X; Y) = D(p(x, y) \| p(x)\,p(y)) = \sum_{x, y} p(x, y)\log_2\frac{p(x, y)}{p(x)p(y)}.\]

Rewriting the KL yields three equivalent expressions: \[I(X; Y) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X, Y) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X) .\]

\(I(X; Y) \geq 0\), with equality iff \(X, Y\) are independent.


A binary symmetric channel with crossover probability \(q\) carries information \(I(X; Y) = 1 - h_2(q)\) per symbol when the input is uniform. At \(q = 0\) (noise-free) it carries the full 1 bit; at \(q = 1/2\) (pure noise) it carries zero.

title: 3  Information-theoretic measures
text:
3.4 Venn-diagram of information
The three quantities \(H(X), H(Y), H(X, Y)\) and their combinations \(H(X \mid Y), H(Y \mid X), I(X; Y)\) obey the same set-theoretic identities as a Venn diagram of two overlapping sets. This is the pedagogical device that generations of textbooks use to remember the relations.

Remark. The Venn-diagram picture breaks for three or more random variables because the “interaction information” \(I(X; Y; Z)\) can be negative. Don’t over-extend the analogy.

title: 3  Information-theoretic measures
text:
3.5 Data-processing inequality
An operational classic: post-processing cannot increase information.

If \(X \to Y \to Z\) is a Markov chain (i.e. \(Z \perp\!\!\!\perp X \mid Y\)), then \[I(X; Y) \geq I(X; Z).\] Equality holds iff \(Y \to Z\) preserves all information about \(X\).

Proof. Use the chain rule \(I(X; Y, Z) = I(X; Y) + I(X; Z \mid Y) = I(X; Z) + I(X; Y \mid Z)\). The Markov property makes \(I(X; Z \mid Y) = 0\), so \(I(X; Y) = I(X; Z) + I(X; Y \mid Z) \geq I(X; Z)\).

title: 3  Information-theoretic measures
text:
3.6 Convexity and further identities

\(D(p \| q)\) is convex in the pair \((p, q)\): for \(\lambda \in [0, 1]\), \[D(\lambda p_1 + (1 - \lambda)p_2 \| \lambda q_1 + (1 - \lambda)q_2) \leq \lambda D(p_1 \| q_1) + (1 - \lambda)D(p_2 \| q_2).\]


For fixed conditional \(p(y \mid x)\), \(I(X; Y)\) is a concave function of \(p(x)\). For fixed marginal \(p(x)\), \(I(X; Y)\) is a convex function of \(p(y \mid x)\). This is the workhorse behind the capacity theorems.

title: 3  Information-theoretic measures
text:
3.7 Exercises

Show that \(H(X, Y) \leq H(X) + H(Y)\) with equality iff \(X, Y\) are independent, using the log-sum inequality directly (not via mutual information).


Solution. Write \(H(X) + H(Y) - H(X, Y) = -\sum_{x,y}p(x,y)\log[p(x)p(y)/p(x,y)]\). By the log-sum inequality applied with \(a_{xy} = p(x,y)\) and \(b_{xy} = p(x)p(y)\), \[\sum_{x,y} p(x,y)\log \tfrac{p(x,y)}{p(x)p(y)} \geq 1 \cdot \log \tfrac{1}{1} = 0.\] So the difference is \(\geq 0\) with equality iff \(p(x,y)/[p(x)p(y)]\) is constant — i.e. equal to 1 — iff independence.


Compute \(I(X; Y)\) for a binary symmetric channel with error probability \(q\) and uniform input.


Solution. \(H(Y) = 1\) (uniform input plus symmetric noise gives uniform output). \(H(Y \mid X) = h_2(q)\) (conditional on the input, \(Y\) is Bernoulli\((q)\)). So \(I(X; Y) = 1 - h_2(q)\), matching the example above.


Prove the data-processing inequality for the specific case \(X \to Y \to Z\) where \(Y = f(X)\) deterministically.


Solution. \(H(X \mid Y) = 0\) because \(Y\) determines \(X\) trivially… wait, if \(Y = f(X)\) then \(X\) is not determined by \(Y\) unless \(f\) is invertible. Instead: \(I(X;Z) = H(X) - H(X|Z) \leq H(X) - H(X|Y,Z)\) (conditioning reduces entropy). Since the Markov property makes \(H(X|Y,Z) = H(X|Y)\), we get \(I(X;Z) \leq H(X) - H(X|Y) = I(X;Y)\). The DPI holds. Deterministic post-processing is a special case.

title: 3  Information-theoretic measures
text:
3.8 Callouts






The three interpretations of mutual information — as a KL divergence, as a reduction of entropy, and as an inclusion–exclusion of joint and marginal entropies — are all useful. Which one you invoke depends on what you want to prove.









When bounding an information quantity, try (i) apply Jensen’s inequality to \(-\log\); (ii) apply the log-sum inequality; (iii) invoke the data-processing inequality. These three moves cover 90% of the proofs in Cover & Thomas.









The KL divergence \(D(p \| q)\) is asymmetric. In machine learning the direction matters: \(D(p \| q)\) (with \(p\) empirical) is maximum-likelihood; \(D(q \| p)\) is not.

title: 4  Source coding: compression
text:
4.1 Two ways to compress
Shannon’s motivation for defining entropy was to answer an engineering question: given a source that emits symbols according to a distribution \(p\), what is the minimum number of bits per symbol needed to transmit them? This chapter proves the two source-coding theorems (lossy and lossless) that make the answer \(H(X)\) operational.
There is a fundamental split in the theory:
The tools for the two problems are different, but both build on the same object: the typical set.

title: 4  Source coding: compression
text:
Lossless compression reconstructs every original symbol exactly. Examples: gzip, PNG, FLAC.
Lossy compression allows some distortion in reconstruction. Examples: JPEG, MP3, H.264.

title: 4  Source coding: compression
text:
4.2 The typical set and AEP

Fix \(\varepsilon > 0\) and \(n \in \mathbb N\). The \(\varepsilon\)-typical set of length-\(n\) sequences from source \(X \sim p\) is \[A_\varepsilon^{(n)} = \Bigl\{ x^n \in \mathcal X^n : \Bigl|\,{-\tfrac{1}{n}\log_2 p(x^n) - H(X)}\Bigr| \leq \varepsilon \Bigr\}.\] That is, sequences whose empirical entropy is close to \(H(X)\).


For \(X_1, X_2, \ldots\) i.i.d. \(\sim p\):

\(-\tfrac{1}{n}\log_2 p(X_1, \ldots, X_n) \to H(X)\) in probability as \(n \to \infty\).
\(P(A_\varepsilon^{(n)}) \to 1\) as \(n \to \infty\).
\(|A_\varepsilon^{(n)}| \leq 2^{n(H(X) + \varepsilon)}\) and \(|A_\varepsilon^{(n)}| \geq (1 - \varepsilon) 2^{n(H(X) - \varepsilon)}\) for \(n\) sufficiently large.


The AEP is the workhorse of Shannon-style theorems: almost all probability mass concentrates on a set of roughly \(2^{nH}\) sequences, and these sequences are (asymptotically) equiprobable — hence the equipartition.

Remark (Physical meaning). The AEP is the information-theoretic analogue of the ergodic theorem: the “typical” behaviour of a long random sequence is the same as the ensemble-averaged behaviour, up to exponentially small corrections.

title: 4  Source coding: compression
text:
4.3 Lossy source coding

Fix \(\varepsilon > 0\). For \(n\) sufficiently large, there exists a code \(\phi_n : \mathcal X^n \to \{0, 1\}^{n(H(X) + \varepsilon)}\) and decoder \(\psi_n\) such that \[P\bigl(\psi_n(\phi_n(X^n)) \neq X^n\bigr) < \varepsilon .\] Conversely, any code with rate \(R < H(X)\) has error probability tending to 1.

Proof sketch. Enumerate the typical set with \(\lceil n(H + \varepsilon)\rceil\) bits and send atypical sequences to a garbage symbol. By AEP the error probability tends to zero. For the converse use Fano’s inequality (below) to show that any rate below \(H\) leaves a positive average distortion.

Compression at rate \(R < H(X)\) is possible only at the cost of a positive distortion; the rate–distortion function \(R(D) = \min_{p(\hat x | x) : \mathbb E d(X, \hat X) \leq D} I(X; \hat X)\) characterises the optimal trade-off for distortion measure \(d\).

title: 4  Source coding: compression
text:
4.4 Lossless source coding: symbol codes
For truly lossless compression the constraint is that the code be uniquely decodable.

A code \(\phi : \mathcal X \to \{0, 1\}^*\) is a prefix code if no codeword is a prefix of another. Prefix codes are instantaneously decodable: the decoder recognises each codeword as soon as its last bit arrives.


A set of codeword lengths \(\ell_1, \ldots, \ell_M\) can be realised by a binary prefix code iff \[\sum_{i=1}^{M} 2^{-\ell_i} \leq 1 .\]

Proof. Represent codewords as leaves of a binary tree; a length-\(\ell_i\) leaf occupies a fraction \(2^{-\ell_i}\) of the tree. Prefix-free means the leaves are disjoint, so their measures sum to at most 1. Conversely, given lengths satisfying the inequality, greedily place codewords in a binary tree from shortest to longest.

Kraft’s inequality holds for the strictly larger class of uniquely decodable codes — no gain in achievable code lengths by relaxing the prefix condition.

title: 4  Source coding: compression
section: 4.5 Source coding theorem for symbol codes
text:
4.5 Source coding theorem for symbol codes

For any uniquely decodable code \(\phi : \mathcal X \to \{0, 1\}^*\) with expected length \(L = \sum_x p(x)\ell_x\), \[L \geq H(X)/\log_2 2 = H(X) \quad \text{bits/symbol}.\] Conversely there exists a prefix code (a Shannon–Fano code) with \(L < H(X) + 1\).

Proof. Lower bound via Kraft + Gibbs’ inequality; upper bound by choosing \(\ell_x = \lceil \log_2 (1/p(x))\rceil\).

For \(X\) with distribution \((0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.125)\): pick \(\ell = (1, 2, 3, 3)\), so codewords \(0, 10, 110, 111\). Expected length \(L = 0.5 + 0.5 + 0.375 + 0.375 = 1.75\) bits. This exactly matches \(H(X) = 1.75\) bits — a rare case where a simple construction is optimal.

title: 4  Source coding: compression
text:
4.6 Huffman codes
Shannon–Fano codes are simple but not always optimal. Huffman’s greedy algorithm produces an optimal prefix code for a given source distribution.

Given probabilities \(p_1, \ldots, p_M\):

Repeatedly combine the two lowest-probability symbols into a super-symbol whose probability is their sum.
Assign bits 0 and 1 to the merged edges.
Read the codeword for each leaf by traversing from root to leaf.



The expected length of a Huffman code satisfies \[H(X) \leq L^{Huff} < H(X) + 1,\] and no prefix code (with the same source distribution) has smaller expected length.

The gap of at most 1 bit is due to the ceiling operation. For long blocks the gap becomes negligible: coding \(n\)-tuples of source symbols achieves expected length within \(1/n\) of the entropy per symbol.

For \(X\) with probabilities \((0.4, 0.35, 0.2, 0.05)\): entropy \(H = 1.74\) bits. Huffman merges \(0.05 + 0.2 = 0.25\), then \(0.25 + 0.35 = 0.60\), then \(0.60 + 0.4 = 1.0\). Codewords: \(0, 10, 110, 111\) with lengths \((1, 2, 3, 3)\); expected length \(L = 1.85\) bits, only \(0.11\) above \(H\).

title: 4  Source coding: compression
text:
4.7 Universal codes
In practice one rarely knows the source distribution in advance. Universal codes (Lempel–Ziv, arithmetic coding, context-tree weighting) achieve entropy rate for the true distribution without knowing it: they estimate the distribution from the observed prefix and adapt on the fly.

The Lempel–Ziv 1977 sliding-window algorithm, applied to a stationary ergodic source of entropy rate \(H_\infty\), achieves an asymptotic compression rate of \(H_\infty\) per symbol as the window grows. No advance knowledge of the source is needed.


Remark. Modern file formats (gzip, bzip2, xz) are variations on Lempel–Ziv and arithmetic coding. The theoretical guarantee that they hit the entropy limit is a Shannon-theorem consequence of the AEP for ergodic sequences.

title: 4  Source coding: compression
text:
4.8 Exercises

Construct a Huffman code for a source with probabilities \((1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, 1/16)\) and verify it achieves \(H(X)\).


Solution. \(H(X) = 1 + 0.5 + 0.375 + 0.25 + 0.25 = 1.875\) bits. Huffman merges: \((1/16 + 1/16) = 1/8\), then \((1/8 + 1/8) = 1/4\), etc. Final codewords: \(0, 10, 110, 1110, 1111\) with lengths \((1, 2, 3, 4, 4)\); expected length \(L = 1/2 + 1/2 + 3/8 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 1.875\) bits. Exactly \(H\) — because all probabilities are dyadic.


Show that Kraft’s inequality implies \(\sum_i 2^{-\ell_i} = 1\) for a complete prefix code (one where every internal node has two children).


Solution. Each leaf \(i\) of the binary tree at depth \(\ell_i\) occupies a fraction \(2^{-\ell_i}\) of the tree, and a complete binary tree has its leaves partitioning the entire tree, so \(\sum_i 2^{-\ell_i} = 1\). An incomplete code (missing some leaves) gives strict inequality.


Compute \(R(D)\) for a Gaussian source with variance \(\sigma^2\) and squared-error distortion \(d(x, \hat x) = (x - \hat x)^2\).


Solution. The rate–distortion function is \(R(D) = \tfrac12 \log_2(\sigma^2/D)\) for \(0 \leq D \leq \sigma^2\), and \(R(D) = 0\) for \(D \geq \sigma^2\). It is achieved by a jointly Gaussian test channel with reverse-water-filling on the eigenvalues.

title: 4  Source coding: compression
text:
4.9 Callouts






The source-coding theorem is asymptotic: it says the entropy is achievable in the limit of long blocks. Finite-block codes always leave a gap, typically \(O(\log n / n)\).









For a single-symbol Huffman code the code length is \(\lceil \log_2 (1/p_i) \rceil\); if this is not achievable, the gap is at most 1 bit and vanishes for long-block codes.









Real-world compressors use arithmetic coding rather than Huffman when the source distribution has one very-high-probability symbol, because arithmetic coding can produce non-integer code lengths and achieve entropy exactly.









Universal codes give the asymptotic compression rate. On short inputs (a single tweet) they often expand the data due to header overhead. Don’t benchmark compressors on toy examples.

title: 5  Noisy channels and coding
text:
5.1 Decoding as inference
Shannon’s second big theorem answers a complementary question: given a noisy channel, what is the maximum rate at which information can be transmitted with vanishing error probability? The answer is the channel capacity \(C = \max_{p(x)} I(X; Y)\), and its achievability is proved by the beautiful random-coding argument.
Consider a channel \(p(y \mid x)\): an input symbol \(x\) is transmitted and a possibly-corrupted output \(y\) is observed. The decoder’s task is to infer what was sent given what was received.

title: 5  Noisy channels and coding
text:
A discrete memoryless channel (DMC) is a triple \((\mathcal X, \mathcal Y, p(y \mid x))\): input alphabet \(\mathcal X\), output alphabet \(\mathcal Y\), and a conditional distribution \(p(y \mid x)\). Memoryless means for a length-\(n\) transmission, \[p(y^n \mid x^n) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} p(y_i \mid x_i).\]


The BSC with crossover probability \(q \in [0, 1/2]\) has \(\mathcal X = \mathcal Y = \{0, 1\}\) and \(p(1 \mid 0) = p(0 \mid 1) = q\). It flips each bit independently with probability \(q\).


The BEC with erasure probability \(\varepsilon\) has \(\mathcal Y = \{0, 1, ?\}\) and \(p(? \mid x) = \varepsilon\), \(p(x \mid x) = 1 - \varepsilon\). Each input is either received correctly or lost — but never silently corrupted.

title: 5  Noisy channels and coding
text:
5.2 Error-correcting codes
The idea of coding is to send a codeword \(\mathbf x = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)\) chosen from a codebook \(\mathcal C \subset \mathcal X^n\) of size \(|\mathcal C| = 2^{nR}\), so the code rate is \(R = (\log_2 |\mathcal C|)/n\) bits per channel use. On the receiver side, a decoder \(g : \mathcal Y^n \to \mathcal C\) maps the received sequence back to a codeword.

A rate \(R\) is achievable on channel \(p(y \mid x)\) if there exists a sequence of codes \(\{\mathcal C_n\}\) of size \(\lfloor 2^{nR}\rfloor\) and decoders \(\{g_n\}\) such that the maximal error probability \[\lambda^{(n)} = \max_{\mathbf x \in \mathcal C_n} P\bigl(g_n(Y^n) \neq \mathbf x \mid X^n = \mathbf x\bigr)\] tends to zero as \(n \to \infty\). The capacity \(C\) is the supremum of achievable rates.

title: 5  Noisy channels and coding
text:
5.3 The noisy-channel coding theorem

For a discrete memoryless channel, \[C = \max_{p(x)} I(X; Y).\] Any rate \(R < C\) is achievable, and any rate \(R > C\) is not.

Proof idea (achievability). Fix an input distribution \(p(x)\) achieving \(I(X; Y)\). Generate a random codebook of \(2^{nR}\) i.i.d. \(\sim p^{\otimes n}\) codewords. Decode by joint typicality: given \(Y^n\), output the unique codeword \(\hat X^n\) such that \((X^n, Y^n) \in A_\varepsilon^{(n)}\). The average error probability, averaged over both the message and the random codebook, tends to zero for \(R < C - 2\varepsilon\). Then expurgate half the codebook to get a code with maximal error probability tending to zero.
Proof idea (converse). Use Fano’s inequality: \(H(\mathbf X \mid \hat{\mathbf X}) \leq 1 + P_e \cdot nR\), which combined with data processing gives \(nR \leq nC + 1 + nRP_e\), so \(R \leq C\) if \(P_e \to 0\).

For the BSC with crossover \(q\), the capacity is \(C = 1 - h_2(q)\), achieved by uniform \(p(x)\). For the BEC with erasure \(\varepsilon\), \(C = 1 - \varepsilon\): each non-erased symbol conveys one bit.

title: 5  Noisy channels and coding
text:
5.4 Fano’s inequality

Let \(X\) take values in \(\mathcal X\) and let \(\hat X\) be an estimate of \(X\) from any random variable \(Y\). Let \(P_e = P(\hat X \neq X)\). Then \[H(X \mid Y) \leq H(X \mid \hat X) \leq h_2(P_e) + P_e\log_2(|\mathcal X| - 1).\]

Fano’s inequality lower-bounds the error probability of any estimator: if \(P_e\) is small then \(H(X \mid Y)\) must be small too. It is the fundamental tool for converse coding theorems throughout the notes.

Combining Fano with the data-processing inequality yields the converse of the noisy-channel coding theorem: any code with rate above capacity has average error probability bounded away from zero.

title: 5  Noisy channels and coding
text:
5.5 Random coding
The genius of Shannon’s proof is to show existence by averaging. The typical codebook is bad in ways that are hard to see, but the ensemble of codebooks has good average behaviour — so at least one codebook must be at least as good as the average.

For \(R < C\), the average error probability over random codebooks decays exponentially in \(n\): \[\bar P_e \leq 2^{-n(E_r(R))},\] where \(E_r(R) > 0\) for \(R < C\) is Gallager’s random-coding exponent. This gives the sharp asymptotic rate of convergence, not just the fact that it holds.


Remark. The random-coding exponent is what makes Shannon’s theorem quantitative: it tells you how large \(n\) has to be for a given target error. Modern coding theory is largely the search for structured codes that meet or approach the random-coding exponent with efficient encoders and decoders (turbo codes, LDPC, polar codes).

title: 5  Noisy channels and coding
text:
5.6 Typical-set decoding

Given \(p(x, y)\), the jointly typical set \(A_\varepsilon^{(n)}(X, Y)\) is \[\Bigl\{ (x^n, y^n) : |\!-\tfrac{1}{n}\log p(x^n) - H(X)| < \varepsilon,\ |\!-\tfrac{1}{n}\log p(y^n) - H(Y)| < \varepsilon,\ |\!-\tfrac{1}{n}\log p(x^n, y^n) - H(X, Y)| < \varepsilon \Bigr\}.\]


As \(n \to \infty\): (i) \(P((X^n, Y^n) \in A_\varepsilon^{(n)}) \to 1\); (ii) \(|A_\varepsilon^{(n)}(X, Y)| \leq 2^{n(H(X,Y) + \varepsilon)}\); (iii) if \((\tilde X^n, \tilde Y^n)\) are drawn independently from the marginals, then \(P((\tilde X^n, \tilde Y^n) \in A_\varepsilon^{(n)}) \leq 2^{-n(I(X;Y) - 3\varepsilon)}\).

Property (iii) is the key to the noisy-channel coding theorem: it says that if you draw two random \(n\)-sequences from the marginals, they almost never look typical together — the probability of a “spurious match” is exponentially small in \(nI(X; Y)\).

title: 5  Noisy channels and coding
text:
5.7 Structured codes
The random-coding proof does not construct a specific code; it shows one exists. Practical coding requires structured codes with fast decoders.

Send each bit \(n\) times, majority-decode. For a BSC\((q)\) this has rate \(R = 1/n\) and error probability \(\sim \exp(-n D(1/2 \| q))\). Poor rate but easy analysis; a textbook baseline.


Four data bits, three parity bits, minimum distance \(3\): corrects any single error in a block of \(7\). Rate \(R = 4/7\); a first example of an algebraic code that meets the Singleton bound.

Modern codes — LDPC (Gallager 1962), turbo codes (Berrou et al. 1993), polar codes (Arıkan 2009) — approach capacity within fractions of a dB and are decoded in polynomial time. Their invention represents 60 years of work catching up with Shannon.

title: 5  Noisy channels and coding
text:
5.8 Exercises

Compute the capacity of the Z-channel: \(\mathcal X = \mathcal Y = \{0, 1\}\), \(p(0 \mid 0) = 1\), \(p(0 \mid 1) = q\), \(p(1 \mid 1) = 1 - q\).


Solution. Let the input distribution be \(p(0) = \alpha\), \(p(1) = 1 - \alpha\). Then \(H(Y \mid X) = (1 - \alpha) h_2(q)\) and \(H(Y) = h_2(\alpha + (1-\alpha)q)\) (Bernoulli output). Maximise \(I = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X)\) over \(\alpha\). The optimum satisfies a transcendental equation solvable numerically; e.g. for \(q = 0.5\) the capacity is \(\approx 0.322\) bit per channel use, less than the BSC\((0.5)\) capacity (which is zero) — the Z-channel is asymmetric and therefore useful even at large error rates.


Prove Fano’s inequality using the identity \(H(X, \hat X) = H(\hat X) + H(X \mid \hat X)\) and a careful decomposition of \(H(X \mid \hat X)\) into “the error event” and “given the error event”.


Solution. Introduce indicator \(E = \mathbf 1[\hat X \neq X]\). Then \(H(E, X \mid \hat X) = H(E \mid \hat X) + H(X \mid E, \hat X) \leq h_2(P_e) + P_e \log_2(|\mathcal X| - 1)\) (given error, \(X\) is one of the \(|\mathcal X| - 1\) remaining values). Since \(H(X \mid \hat X) \leq H(E, X \mid \hat X)\), the inequality follows.

title: 5  Noisy channels and coding
text:
5.9 Callouts






The noisy-channel coding theorem is the result of information theory: it establishes an operational meaning of mutual information as the maximum rate of reliable communication.









For an asymmetric channel it is often useful to first find \(p(x)\) that maximises \(I(X; Y)\) numerically, then compute the resulting capacity. Symmetric channels admit closed-form solutions.









Shannon’s theorem is an existence result. Constructing capacity-achieving codes was an open problem for decades; even now the practical gap is a few tenths of a dB for high-noise regimes.









The capacity \(C\) is an asymptotic (long-block) quantity. Finite-block coding has a lower achievable rate, characterised by the finite-block-length coding bounds of Polyanskiy, Poor & Verdú (2010).

title: 6  Continuous random variables
text:
6.1 Differential entropy
Shannon’s theory extends naturally from discrete to continuous alphabets, but with a twist: continuous entropies can be negative, and the operational meaning of differential entropy is more subtle than that of Shannon entropy. This chapter introduces the differential entropy, the mutual information of continuous variables, and the Gaussian channel — the paradigm of a continuous-alphabet system.
The formula is the natural continuous analogue of the discrete Shannon entropy, but its interpretation is different:

title: 6  Continuous random variables
text:
For a random variable \(X\) with density \(f_X(x)\), the differential entropy is \[h(X) = -\int f_X(x)\,\log_2 f_X(x)\,dx,\] provided the integral exists.



Remark. \(h(X)\) is not the average number of bits to describe \(X\): continuous variables need infinitely many bits to describe with arbitrary precision. Instead, \(h(X)\) measures the entropy of \(X\) relative to a uniform reference on unit intervals: quantising \(X\) to precision \(\Delta\) gives a discrete variable with entropy \(h(X) - \log_2 \Delta\). The negative differential entropy of a very concentrated density corresponds to a discrete variable that is easier to encode than a uniform bin of size \(\Delta\).


For \(X \sim \text{Unif}[0, a]\): \(h(X) = \log_2 a\). Note \(h < 0\) if \(a < 1\).
For \(X \sim \mathcal N(\mu, \sigma^2)\): \(h(X) = \tfrac12 \log_2(2\pi e\,\sigma^2)\), independent of \(\mu\).

title: 6  Continuous random variables
text:
6.2 Basic properties
Many properties of Shannon entropy carry over unchanged, but with two important exceptions:


\(h(X)\) can be negative (see uniform example).
Scaling: \(h(aX) = h(X) + \log_2 |a|\); translation: \(h(X + c) = h(X)\).
Sub-additivity: \(h(X, Y) \leq h(X) + h(Y)\), equality iff \(X, Y\) independent.
Chain rule: \(h(X, Y) = h(X) + h(Y \mid X)\).
Conditioning reduces entropy: \(h(Y \mid X) \leq h(Y)\).

title: 6  Continuous random variables
text:
6.3 Maximum-entropy distributions
Discrete entropies are maximised by the uniform distribution. Continuous ones are maximised by distributions determined by the given constraints:

Among all real random variables with variance \(\sigma^2\), the Gaussian \(\mathcal N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) has the largest differential entropy \(h = \tfrac12 \log_2(2\pi e \sigma^2)\).

Proof. Use Gibbs’ inequality: for any density \(f\) with the given variance, \[D(f \| f_{\mathcal N}) = h(f_{\mathcal N}) - h(f) \geq 0,\] where the identity uses only \(\int f x^2 dx = \sigma^2\) and \(\int f = 1\).


Bounded support \([a, b]\): uniform maximises \(h\) with \(h = \log_2(b - a)\).
Non-negative support, fixed mean \(\mu\): exponential maximises \(h\) with \(h = \log_2(e\,\mu)\).
Fixed first and second moments: Gaussian maximises.

title: 6  Continuous random variables
text:
6.4 Mutual information for continuous variables

For jointly-distributed \((X, Y)\) with joint density \(f(x, y)\), \[I(X; Y) = \int\!\int f(x, y)\log_2\frac{f(x, y)}{f(x)\,f(y)}\,dx\,dy .\]

Unlike differential entropy, \(I(X; Y) \geq 0\) for continuous variables as well — the KL-divergence structure survives the limit.

\(I(X; Y)\) is invariant under invertible smooth transformations of \(X\) and \(Y\) separately: for diffeomorphisms \(\phi, \psi\), \[I(\phi(X); \psi(Y)) = I(X; Y).\] This is what makes \(I\) a reparameterisation-invariant measure of dependence.

title: 6  Continuous random variables
text:
6.5 The Gaussian channel

The additive Gaussian noise channel with power constraint \(P\) is \[Y = X + Z, \qquad Z \sim \mathcal N(0, N),\quad \mathbb E[X^2] \leq P .\] The average power of the transmitted signal is bounded by \(P\); the noise has variance \(N\); both are per channel use.


The capacity of the Gaussian channel is \[C = \tfrac12 \log_2\bigl(1 + P/N\bigr) \quad \text{bits/channel use.}\] The maximising input distribution is \(X \sim \mathcal N(0, P)\).

Proof. Bound \(I(X; Y) = h(Y) - h(Y \mid X) = h(Y) - h(Z)\). Since \(\text{Var}(Y) = \text{Var}(X) + N \leq P + N\) and Gaussian maximises entropy for a given variance, \(h(Y) \leq \tfrac12\log_2(2\pi e (P + N))\), with equality iff \(Y\) Gaussian, iff \(X\) Gaussian. Then \(C = \tfrac12\log_2(2\pi e(P+N)) - \tfrac12\log_2(2\pi e N) = \tfrac12 \log_2(1 + P/N)\).

For a channel of bandwidth \(B\) Hz and noise spectral density \(N_0 / 2\), the (Shannon–Hartley) capacity is \[C = B\,\log_2\bigl(1 + P/(N_0 B)\bigr) \quad \text{bits/second}.\] This is the celebrated formula relating bandwidth, SNR, and channel capacity that governs everything from modem design to DSL to Wi-Fi.

title: 6  Continuous random variables
text:
6.6 Parallel Gaussian channels and water-filling
For a bank of \(K\) parallel independent Gaussian channels with individual noise variances \(N_i\) and a total power budget \(\sum P_i \leq P\):

The capacity is \[C = \sum_{i=1}^{K} \tfrac12 \log_2\bigl(1 + P_i/N_i\bigr),\] maximised by allocating power \(P_i = \max(0, \mu - N_i)\), where \(\mu\) is the water level chosen so that \(\sum_i P_i = P\).

The intuition: pour a total volume \(P\) of “water” over containers of depths \(N_i\); deeper containers (nosier channels) receive less water.

Remark (Water-filling in modern communications). Water-filling is what OFDM, DSL, LTE, and 5G do at the physical layer: split the frequency band into sub-carriers with individual SNRs, allocate transmit power to maximise total throughput.

title: 6  Continuous random variables
text:
6.7 Exercises

Compute the differential entropy of a Laplace\((\mu, b)\) distribution \(f(x) = (2b)^{-1}\exp(-|x - \mu|/b)\).


Solution. \(h(X) = -\int f \log_2 f = -\int f \log_2\frac{1}{2b} + \log_2 e \int f\,|x - \mu|/b\, dx = \log_2(2b) + \log_2 e\). So \(h = \log_2(2b\,e)\) bits. Interesting comparison: for the same variance \(2b^2\), the Gaussian has entropy \(\tfrac12\log_2(2\pi e \cdot 2b^2) = \tfrac12\log_2(4\pi e b^2)\); Laplace has \(h = \log_2(2be) = \tfrac12 \log_2(4b^2 e^2)\). Ratio: Gaussian is larger by factor \(\log_2(\pi/e) \approx 0.20\) bits — Gaussian is the max-ent distribution.


For the Gaussian channel with SNR = 10 dB, compute the capacity in bits/s/Hz.


Solution. \(C = \log_2(1 + 10) = \log_2 11 \approx 3.46\) bits/s/Hz. Modern LTE aims to reach \(\sim 90\%\) of this in the physical layer with efficient turbo/LDPC coding.


Verify that among Gaussian variables the Fisher information \(J(f) = \mathbb E[(\partial_x \log f)^2]\) satisfies \(J(f) = 1/\sigma^2\) and that the entropy-Fisher information identity \(J(f) \geq 2\pi e \cdot 2^{-2h(f)}\) holds with equality iff Gaussian.


Solution. Direct: \(\partial_x \log \mathcal N(x; 0, \sigma^2) = -x/\sigma^2\), so \(J = 1/\sigma^2\). Substituting the Gaussian \(h = \tfrac12 \log_2(2\pi e\sigma^2)\): \(2\pi e \cdot 2^{-2h} = 2\pi e / (2\pi e \sigma^2) = 1/\sigma^2 = J\). This is the Stam / Blachman inequality — a Cramér–Rao-like bound in disguise.

title: 6  Continuous random variables
text:
6.8 Callouts






Differential entropy is a coordinate-dependent quantity: change of variable \(Y = g(X)\) gives \(h(Y) = h(X) + \mathbb E[\log |g'(X)|]\). Only quantities like \(I(X; Y)\) and KL are coordinate-free.









When you need entropy for a continuous variable, first check whether it fits a maximum-entropy family (Gaussian, exponential, uniform); those admit closed-form answers. Otherwise, quantise and use the discrete entropy formula.









Negative differential entropy is not a sign of an error: it just means the distribution is more concentrated than a unit-support uniform. It becomes a positive quantity again when converted to a discrete entropy at any finite resolution.









The Gaussian capacity \(\tfrac12\log_2(1 + \text{SNR})\) is the practical benchmark of digital communication systems. Anything above it violates Shannon; anything close to it is state-of-the-art coding.

title: 7  Markov chains and information in time series
text:
7.1 Markov chains
The information framework of the previous chapters treated symbols as i.i.d. Real data are almost never i.i.d.: language has grammar, DNA has motifs, prices have trends. To measure the information content of a sequence with memory we need to consider stochastic processes — Markov chains are the simplest interesting case.
crumbs: 7  Markov chains and information in time series

title: 7  Markov chains and information in time series
text:
A discrete-time Markov chain on state space \(\mathcal S\) is a sequence \(\{X_t\}_{t \geq 0}\) such that \[P(X_{t+1} = s' \mid X_t = s, X_{t-1}, \ldots, X_0) = P(X_{t+1} = s' \mid X_t = s) = T(s, s'),\] where \(T\) is the transition matrix. The distribution at time \(t\) evolves as \(\pi_{t+1} = \pi_t\,T\).


A distribution \(\pi^*\) is stationary for \(T\) if \(\pi^* = \pi^*\,T\). If additionally \[\pi^*(s)\,T(s, s') = \pi^*(s')\,T(s', s) \quad \forall s, s',\] the chain satisfies detailed balance and is called reversible.


An irreducible, aperiodic Markov chain on a finite state space has a unique stationary distribution \(\pi^*\), and \(\pi_t \to \pi^*\) geometrically as \(t \to \infty\), from any initial distribution.
crumbs: 7  Markov chains and information in time series

title: 7  Markov chains and information in time series
text:
7.2 Entropy rate
For a stochastic process the entropy of a single symbol undersells the information: correlations between successive symbols mean each new symbol conveys less information than the marginal entropy suggests.

The entropy rate of a stationary process \(\{X_t\}\) is \[H_\infty(X) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} H(X_1, \ldots, X_n) = \lim_{n \to \infty} H(X_n \mid X_1, \ldots, X_{n-1}),\] whenever the limit exists. For a Markov chain the entropy rate simplifies to \[H_\infty(X) = H(X_2 \mid X_1) = \sum_s \pi^*(s)\,H(T(s, \cdot)).\]


Shannon’s own experiments (1951) estimated the entropy rate of English text at \(\sim 1{-}1.5\) bits per letter — much lower than the naive \(\log_2 26 \approx 4.7\) bits/letter — because of strong statistical dependencies between letters, words and grammar. This is exactly the compression ratio (~5–6×) that modern text compressors achieve.


Remark. The entropy rate is the asymptotic compression bound: a universal code can compress a long ergodic sequence at rate arbitrarily close to \(H_\infty\), but no less.
crumbs: 7  Markov chains and information in time series

title: 7  Markov chains and information in time series
text:
7.3 Entropy production in Markov chains
Physicists care about a related quantity: the entropy produced by a non-equilibrium chain per step.

For a Markov chain with transition matrix \(T\) and stationary distribution \(\pi^*\), the entropy production rate is \[\sigma = \sum_{s, s'}\pi^*(s)\,T(s, s')\,\log\frac{T(s, s')}{T(s', s)}.\] Equivalently, \(\sigma = \sum_{s, s'}\pi^*(s)T(s, s')\log\frac{\pi^*(s)T(s, s')}{\pi^*(s')T(s', s)}\): the KL divergence between forward and reverse trajectory distributions.


\(\sigma \geq 0\), with equality iff detailed balance holds. Non-zero entropy production is the information-theoretic signature of non-equilibrium (breaking of time-reversal symmetry).
crumbs: 7  Markov chains and information in time series

title: 7  Markov chains and information in time series
text:
7.4 Hidden Markov models
Often the state of interest is not directly observable: a hidden state \(S_t\) emits an observed symbol \(Y_t\) through an emission distribution \(p(y \mid s)\). This is a hidden Markov model (HMM).

An HMM is a pair \((\{S_t\}, \{Y_t\})\) where \(\{S_t\}\) is a Markov chain on \(\mathcal S\) and each \(Y_t\) is emitted independently given \(S_t\) from a distribution \(p(y \mid s)\).

Standard HMM problems — inference of \(S_t\) from \(Y_1, \ldots, Y_T\) (forward-backward, Viterbi) and learning \(T\) and emission parameters (Baum–Welch, i.e. EM) — are all instances of general inference algorithms on trees or chains, and their information-theoretic complexity is well-studied.

Gene-finding algorithms model the DNA as an HMM with hidden states \(S_t \in \{\text{exon, intron, intergenic, \ldots}\}\) and observed nucleotides \(Y_t \in \{A, C, G, T\}\). Viterbi decoding assigns the most likely state sequence — a genomic annotation.
crumbs: 7  Markov chains and information in time series

title: 7  Markov chains and information in time series
text:
7.5 Spectrum of a Markov chain
The rate at which a Markov chain approaches stationarity is set by the second-largest eigenvalue of its transition matrix:

For a reversible chain with eigenvalues \(1 = \lambda_1 > \lambda_2 \geq \ldots \geq \lambda_{|\mathcal S|}\), the total-variation distance to stationarity satisfies \[\|\pi_t - \pi^*\|_{TV} \leq \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{|\mathcal S|}\,\lambda_2^t .\] The spectral gap \(1 - \lambda_2\) controls the rate of convergence; the mixing time is \(t_{mix} \sim (\log |\mathcal S|)/(1 - \lambda_2)\).
crumbs: 7  Markov chains and information in time series

title: 7  Markov chains and information in time series
text:
7.6 Convergence and independence
For an ergodic chain successive states become approximately independent at long lags, in the sense that \[I(X_t; X_{t+k}) \to 0 \text{ as } k \to \infty ,\] at a rate governed by the spectral gap. This mixing property is what makes long-run averages over a chain trajectory approximate expectations under \(\pi^*\) — the basis of Markov Chain Monte Carlo (Chapter 7).

For an ergodic chain with stationary distribution \(\pi^*\) and any bounded \(f : \mathcal S \to \mathbb R\), \[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n} f(X_t) \to \sum_s \pi^*(s)\,f(s) = \mathbb E_{\pi^*}[f]\] almost surely as \(n \to \infty\).
crumbs: 7  Markov chains and information in time series

title: 7  Markov chains and information in time series
text:
7.7 Autocorrelation
The autocorrelation of a Markov-chain observable decays exponentially in the lag:

For a reversible chain, the autocorrelation of \(f\) satisfies \[C_f(k) = \mathbb E_{\pi^*}[f(X_0) f(X_k)] - \mathbb E_{\pi^*}[f]^2 = \sum_{i \geq 2} \langle f, e_i\rangle^2\,\lambda_i^k,\] where \(\{e_i\}\) are the eigenvectors of \(T\) orthonormalised in \(\ell^2(\pi^*)\). The dominant term decays as \(\lambda_2^k\).


Remark (Effective sample size). The integrated autocorrelation time \(\tau_f = 1 + 2\sum_{k \geq 1} C_f(k)/C_f(0)\) measures how many “independent” samples an \(n\)-step chain provides. The effective sample size is \(n/\tau_f\). Diagnosing large \(\tau_f\) is the main tool for identifying poor MCMC mixing.
crumbs: 7  Markov chains and information in time series

title: 7  Markov chains and information in time series
text:
7.8 Exercises

For a two-state Markov chain on \(\{0, 1\}\) with transition probabilities \(T(0, 1) = a\) and \(T(1, 0) = b\), find the stationary distribution and entropy rate.


Solution. \(\pi^*(0) = b/(a + b)\), \(\pi^*(1) = a/(a + b)\). Entropy rate: \[H_\infty = \frac{b}{a+b}h_2(a) + \frac{a}{a+b}h_2(b).\]


Compute the entropy production of a three-state cyclic chain with rates \(T(0 \to 1) = T(1 \to 2) = T(2 \to 0) = p\) (forward) and equal \(q\) (backward), \(p + q < 1\).


Solution. By symmetry \(\pi^* = (1/3, 1/3, 1/3)\), and \[\sigma = 3 \cdot \tfrac13 \cdot p \log \tfrac{p}{q} + 3 \cdot \tfrac13 \cdot q \log \tfrac{q}{p} = (p - q)\log(p/q).\] Note \(\sigma > 0\) iff \(p \neq q\), and equals zero iff the chain is at detailed balance.


Show that for a reversible chain, \(\lambda_2\) satisfies \(\lambda_2 = 1 - 2\lambda_2^{eff}\) where \(\lambda_2^{eff}\) is the smallest positive eigenvalue of the graph Laplacian of \(T\). Interpret physically.


Solution. Detailed balance \(\pi^*(s)T(s, s') = \pi^*(s')T(s', s)\) makes the symmetric operator \(L = I - T\) self-adjoint in \(\ell^2(\pi^*)\); its spectrum is \(\{1 - \lambda_i\}\). The gap \(1 - \lambda_2\) is the smallest positive eigenvalue of the graph Laplacian — a Cheeger-type quantity that lower-bounds the conductance of the chain. Physically it is the relaxation rate of the slowest mode.

title: 7  Markov chains and information in time series
text:
7.9 Callouts






Markov chains give an analytical framework for time series that fits neatly into information theory. Real time series (financial, biological) are only approximately Markov, but the framework is a useful null model.









When estimating an entropy rate from data, always use a conditional entropy estimator: naive plug-in estimation of \(H(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) has severe bias in high dimensions.









Long correlations kill mixing: chains with \(\lambda_2\) very close to 1 need exponentially many samples to converge and are effectively unusable as samplers. Always diagnose with \(\tau_f\) before trusting an MCMC estimate.

title: 8  Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Metropolis
text:
8.1 The Monte Carlo approach
Suppose we want to compute an expectation \(\mathbb E_\pi[f]\) against a distribution \(\pi\) we can evaluate only up to a normalisation constant — a Bayesian posterior, or a Boltzmann distribution in high dimension. Direct integration is impossible; independent sampling is impossible; but dependent sampling via a cleverly-designed Markov chain works. This chapter introduces the Metropolis algorithm and its theoretical justification.
The core Monte Carlo idea is dead simple:
The rate \(1/\sqrt n\) is dimension-free — it does not degrade with the size of \(\mathcal X\). This is the fundamental advantage of Monte Carlo over deterministic quadrature in high dimension.
crumbs: 8  Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Metropolis

title: 8  Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Metropolis
text: Given i.i.d. samples \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim \pi\) and a function \(f : \mathcal X \to \mathbb R\) with finite variance, the Monte Carlo estimator of \(\mathbb E_\pi[f]\) is \[\widehat{\mathbb E}_n[f] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} f(X_i).\] By the law of large numbers \(\widehat{\mathbb E}_n[f] \to \mathbb E_\pi[f]\) a.s.; by the CLT the error is \(O(1/\sqrt n)\).
crumbs: 8  Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Metropolis

title: 8  Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Metropolis
section: 8.2 Simple ways to sample a distribution
text:
8.2 Simple ways to sample a distribution
For low-dimensional or well-structured \(\pi\) there are direct sampling algorithms:

For a real random variable \(X\) with CDF \(F\): draw \(U \sim \text{Unif}(0, 1)\) and set \(X = F^{-1}(U)\). Then \(X \sim F\). Requires \(F^{-1}\) in closed form or via numerical inversion.


To sample \(\pi\), choose a proposal \(q\) with \(\pi(x) \leq M\,q(x)\) for some \(M \geq 1\). Draw \(X \sim q\) and accept with probability \(\pi(X)/(M q(X))\). Accepted samples are exactly \(\sim \pi\). Acceptance probability is \(1/M\); the method fails in high dimension because \(M\) grows exponentially.


Remark. Direct methods fail on the problem that motivates most of Bayesian statistics: sampling from a high-dimensional posterior \(\pi(\boldsymbol\theta \mid \mathbf y) \propto p(\mathbf y \mid \boldsymbol\theta) p(\boldsymbol\theta)\) where the normalisation is intractable. This is where MCMC comes in.
crumbs: 8  Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Metropolis

title: 8  Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Metropolis
text:
8.3 Markov Chain Monte Carlo
The MCMC insight: construct a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is \(\pi\), run it long enough that its state distribution has converged to \(\pi\), and use its trajectory to estimate expectations. The samples \(X_1, X_2, \ldots\) are not independent, but by the ergodic theorem (Chapter 6) time averages still converge to expectations.

Given a Markov chain with stationary distribution \(\pi\) and initial burn-in \(b\), \[\widehat{\mathbb E}_n[f] = \frac{1}{n - b}\sum_{t = b + 1}^{n} f(X_t) \to \mathbb E_\pi[f] \text{ a.s.}\] The finite-sample error scales as \(\sqrt{\tau_f}/\sqrt n\) where \(\tau_f\) is the integrated autocorrelation time of \(f\) (Chapter 6).
crumbs: 8  Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Metropolis

title: 8  Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Metropolis
text:
8.4 The Metropolis algorithm
The workhorse MCMC algorithm is Metropolis (1953) and its Hastings extension:

Given a target \(\pi\) known up to a constant and a proposal \(q(y \mid x)\):

From current state \(X_t = x\), draw a proposal \(y \sim q(\cdot \mid x)\).
Compute the acceptance ratio \[A(x \to y) = \min\left(1,\ \frac{\pi(y)\,q(x \mid y)}{\pi(x)\,q(y \mid x)}\right).\]
Set \(X_{t+1} = y\) with probability \(A(x \to y)\); otherwise \(X_{t+1} = x\).

For a symmetric proposal (\(q(y \mid x) = q(x \mid y)\)), the ratio reduces to \(A = \min(1, \pi(y)/\pi(x))\).


The Metropolis–Hastings kernel \(T(x, y) = q(y \mid x) A(x \to y)\) satisfies detailed balance with respect to \(\pi\): \(\pi(x)T(x, y) = \pi(y)T(y, x)\). Hence \(\pi\) is stationary for the chain.

Proof. Direct computation from the definition of \(A\): the min preserves detailed balance because the acceptance ratio is exactly the ratio of forward to backward flux under \(\pi\otimes q\).

Target \(\pi(x) \propto e^{-x^2/2}\). Proposal: \(y = x + \sigma_p \xi\) with \(\xi \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)\). Acceptance: \(A = \min(1, e^{(x^2 - y^2)/2})\). For \(\sigma_p \approx 2.4\) the chain has \(\sim 24\%\) acceptance and mixes well — this is the theoretical optimum for a 1D Gaussian target.
crumbs: 8  Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Metropolis

title: 8  Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Metropolis
text:
8.5 Tuning the proposal
The step size \(\sigma_p\) of a Gaussian random-walk proposal has a sweet spot:

For a Gaussian random-walk Metropolis on a \(d\)-dimensional target with roughly Gaussian shape, the asymptotically-optimal acceptance rate is \(\alpha^* \approx 0.234\), achieved by scaling \(\sigma_p^2 \propto d^{-1}\).


Remark. The rule of thumb “aim for 20–40% acceptance” comes from this result and works surprisingly well across problems. Too-small \(\sigma_p\) gives \(\alpha \to 1\) but the chain crawls; too-large gives \(\alpha \to 0\) and the chain sticks at the current state.
crumbs: 8  Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Metropolis

title: 8  Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Metropolis
text:
8.6 Practical Metropolis

Suppose we want to sample the posterior of a Bayesian linear regression \(y_i = \boldsymbol\beta^\top \mathbf x_i + \varepsilon_i\) with a Gaussian likelihood and an informative Gaussian prior on \(\boldsymbol\beta\). The unnormalised posterior is \[\pi(\boldsymbol\beta) \propto \exp\Bigl(-\tfrac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_i(y_i - \boldsymbol\beta^\top \mathbf x_i)^2 - \tfrac{1}{2\tau^2}\|\boldsymbol\beta\|^2\Bigr).\] A Gaussian random-walk Metropolis proposal on \(\boldsymbol\beta\) with \(\sigma_p^2 = 2.4^2/d\) times a preconditioner will typically converge in \(\sim 10^4\) iterations.
crumbs: 8  Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Metropolis

title: 8  Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Metropolis
text:
8.7 Multi-move / block updates
For high-dimensional targets, updating all coordinates jointly in a random-walk Metropolis has poor scaling. Two remedies:

Update each coordinate \(x_j\) separately, holding the others fixed. Each move accepts or rejects based on the conditional target \(\pi(x_j \mid x_{-j})\).

Component-wise updates are the Gibbs sampler of Chapter 8 in the limit that the conditional proposal is the conditional target.

For a target of the form \(\pi(\mathbf x) \propto e^{-U(\mathbf x)}\), HMC augments the state with a momentum variable and proposes \(\mathbf x \to \mathbf x'\) by running Hamilton’s equations of the augmented system, then does a Metropolis accept/reject on the joint energy. The proposal preserves the target and mixes at a rate that scales as \(O(d^{1/4})\) rather than \(O(d^{-1})\) for random walk.


Remark. HMC / NUTS is the algorithm behind Stan, PyMC and TensorFlow Probability. Its efficient handling of geometry via momentum is why it dominates modern Bayesian inference on continuous parameters.
crumbs: 8  Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Metropolis

title: 8  Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Metropolis
text:
8.8 Diagnostics
Verifying convergence of an MCMC run is a subtle empirical exercise. The standard tools are:

Trace plots of \(f(X_t)\) vs \(t\): should look like white noise around a stationary mean.
Effective sample size (ESS): \(n_{\text{eff}} = n / (1 + 2\sum_{k \geq 1}\hat\rho(k))\); ratios below \(0.1\) signal poor mixing.
Gelman–Rubin \(\hat R\): run \(M\) chains from over-dispersed starts and compare within-chain and between-chain variance. \(\hat R < 1.01\) is the modern convergence threshold.







Never trust an MCMC estimate from a single chain. Always run at least four in parallel, and inspect \(\hat R\) before quoting a posterior number.
crumbs: 8  Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Metropolis

title: 8  Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Metropolis
text:
8.9 Exercises

Simulate a Metropolis chain for a 2D banana-shaped target \(\pi(x, y) \propto \exp(-x^2/10 - (y - x^2/10)^2/2)\). Estimate the effective sample size for the second component.


Solution. A random-walk Metropolis with isotropic proposal has ESS \(\sim 10^2\) per \(10^4\) steps because the banana shape defeats isotropic scaling. HMC or preconditioning brings ESS \(\sim 10^3\) or better. This is the standard illustration in the Stan documentation of why HMC dominates for non-elliptical posteriors.


Prove that if \(q(y \mid x) = q(x \mid y)\) then the Metropolis-Hastings acceptance probability reduces to \(A = \min(1, \pi(y)/\pi(x))\), and verify detailed balance in this simplified form.


Solution. Substituting \(q(y|x) = q(x|y)\) into the Hastings formula makes the \(q\) terms cancel. Detailed balance: \(\pi(x) T(x,y) = \pi(x) q(y|x) \min(1, \pi(y)/\pi(x)) = q(y|x) \min(\pi(x), \pi(y)) = q(x|y) \min(\pi(x), \pi(y)) = \pi(y) T(y,x)\). ✓
crumbs: 8  Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Metropolis

title: 8  Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Metropolis
text:
8.10 Callouts






Metropolis is not the fastest MCMC algorithm; it is the most general. For specific problems (Gaussian latent variables, hierarchical models), specialised samplers like NUTS or slice-sampling do orders of magnitude better.









The MCMC estimator is biased by the initial burn-in period. Always discard a burn-in and check that discarding more doesn’t change your estimate significantly.









An MCMC chain that “looks converged” in a trace plot may still be missing modes of a multi-modal target. Trace plots detect within-mode stationarity, not between-mode mixing. Multi-modal posteriors need tempered chains or SMC.









Effective sample size is the only number that quantifies MCMC efficiency. Wall-clock time comparisons between samplers are only meaningful when normalised by ESS/sec.

title: 9  Gibbs sampling and high-dimensional inference
text:
9.1 The Gibbs sampling algorithm
Metropolis is universal but blunt. When the target factorises well — Bayesian hierarchical models, mixture models, latent-variable models — a specialised algorithm called Gibbs sampling exploits the structure and dominates. This chapter introduces Gibbs sampling, illustrates it on mixture distributions, and works through a running high-dimensional inference example.
The idea: instead of proposing a full joint move and Metropolising, sample each block of variables exactly from its conditional given the others.
Proof. By construction the conditional draw preserves the joint: sampling \(x_j \sim \pi(\cdot \mid x_{-j})\) and leaving \(x_{-j}\) fixed gives a joint that still integrates to \(\pi(x_j, x_{-j}) = \pi(\mathbf x)\). Detailed balance is verified coordinate-wise.
crumbs: 9  Gibbs sampling and high-dimensional inference

title: 9  Gibbs sampling and high-dimensional inference
text:
Given a joint density \(\pi(\mathbf x) = \pi(x_1, \ldots, x_d)\), the Gibbs sampler updates one coordinate at a time:
For \(t = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\):

Pick coordinate \(j\) (deterministically cycling or uniformly at random).
Sample \(x_j^{(t+1)} \sim \pi(x_j \mid x_{-j}^{(t)})\) where \(x_{-j}\) denotes all coordinates except \(j\).
Set \(x_i^{(t+1)} = x_i^{(t)}\) for \(i \neq j\).



The Gibbs sampler leaves \(\pi\) invariant: if \(\mathbf X^{(t)} \sim \pi\) then \(\mathbf X^{(t+1)} \sim \pi\). Moreover under mild ergodicity assumptions the chain converges to \(\pi\) from any initial state.



Remark. Gibbs sampling is a special case of Metropolis-Hastings with a proposal that is exactly the conditional distribution: acceptance is then always 1. This is the sense in which Gibbs “always accepts”.
crumbs: 9  Gibbs sampling and high-dimensional inference

title: 9  Gibbs sampling and high-dimensional inference
text:
9.2 When Gibbs sampling helps
Gibbs is efficient when the conditionals \(\pi(x_j \mid x_{-j})\) have a familiar form (Gaussian, Dirichlet, categorical) so that we can sample from them exactly. Bayesian models with conjugate priors are the paradigm case.

For the model \(y_i \mid \boldsymbol\beta, \sigma^2 \sim \mathcal N(\boldsymbol\beta^\top \mathbf x_i, \sigma^2)\) with priors \(\boldsymbol\beta \sim \mathcal N(\mathbf 0, \tau^2 I)\) and \(\sigma^2 \sim \text{InvGamma}(\alpha, \beta)\):

\(\pi(\boldsymbol\beta \mid \sigma^2, \mathbf y) = \mathcal N(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta},\ \Sigma_\beta)\) where \(\Sigma_\beta = (\mathbf X^\top \mathbf X/\sigma^2 + I/\tau^2)^{-1}\), \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \Sigma_\beta \mathbf X^\top \mathbf y/\sigma^2\).
\(\pi(\sigma^2 \mid \boldsymbol\beta, \mathbf y) = \text{InvGamma}(\alpha + n/2,\ \beta + \tfrac12 \|\mathbf y - \mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta\|^2)\).

Alternating between the two conjugate updates samples the joint posterior in a few thousand iterations.
crumbs: 9  Gibbs sampling and high-dimensional inference

title: 9  Gibbs sampling and high-dimensional inference
text:
9.3 Mixture distributions
Latent-variable models are the sweet spot of Gibbs sampling. Consider a mixture of \(K\) Gaussians: \[p(y_i \mid \boldsymbol\mu, \sigma^2, \mathbf w) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} w_k\,\mathcal N(y_i; \mu_k, \sigma^2).\]

Introduce a latent cluster indicator \(z_i \in \{1, \ldots, K\}\) for each observation with \(p(z_i = k) = w_k\) and \(p(y_i \mid z_i = k) = \mathcal N(\mu_k, \sigma^2)\). Gibbs sampling then alternates:

Update \(z_i\): sample \(z_i \sim \text{Categorical}(\gamma_{i, 1}, \ldots, \gamma_{i, K})\) with \(\gamma_{i, k} \propto w_k \mathcal N(y_i; \mu_k, \sigma^2)\).
Update \(\mu_k\): sample \(\mu_k\) from its Gaussian posterior given \(\{y_i : z_i = k\}\).
Update \(\mathbf w\): sample from the Dirichlet posterior given the cluster counts \(\{|\{i : z_i = k\}|\}\).

The chain converges rapidly for well-separated components and mixes surprisingly slowly (multi-modality!) for overlapping ones.
crumbs: 9  Gibbs sampling and high-dimensional inference

title: 9  Gibbs sampling and high-dimensional inference
text:
9.4 A basic inference example
We now work through the running example from Prof. Allegra’s notes: inferring a scalar signal \(\theta\) from noisy binary measurements.

Observations \(y_i \in \{0, 1\}\) for \(i = 1, \ldots, n\) are drawn as \(y_i \sim \text{Bern}(\sigma(\theta))\) where \(\sigma(z) = (1 + e^{-z})^{-1}\) is the logistic function. Prior on \(\theta\): \(\theta \sim \mathcal N(0, \tau^2)\).

The unnormalised posterior is \[\pi(\theta \mid \mathbf y) \propto \exp\bigl(-\theta^2/(2\tau^2)\bigr)\prod_i \sigma(\theta)^{y_i}(1 - \sigma(\theta))^{1 - y_i}.\] This is not conjugate: no closed-form update. Two approaches:

Use a Gaussian random-walk proposal \(\theta' = \theta + \sigma_p \xi\) and accept with the standard Metropolis ratio. Even with 10^5 samples the chain converges within a few hundred iterations for typical \(n \sim 100\).


The posterior does not have a closed-form density but its log is \[\log \pi(\theta \mid \mathbf y) = -\theta^2/(2\tau^2) + n_1 \theta - n \log(1 + e^\theta) + \text{const},\] where \(n_1 = \sum_i y_i\). The posterior is unimodal and concave, so a Laplace approximation around its mode gives a good analytic reference.


Simulate \(n = 200\) observations with true \(\theta = 0.5\) and prior \(\tau = 3\). The posterior is centred near \(0.5\) with standard deviation \(\sim 0.15\). Metropolis with \(\sigma_p = 0.3\) yields an acceptance rate \(\sim 40\%\) and an ESS/iteration of \(\sim 0.4\) — respectable for a 1D problem.
crumbs: 9  Gibbs sampling and high-dimensional inference

title: 9  Gibbs sampling and high-dimensional inference
text:
9.5 Refined model: hierarchy
Push the example one level deeper. Suppose the true signal varies across \(G\) groups (a hierarchical model): \[y_{gi} \sim \text{Bern}(\sigma(\theta_g)),\qquad \theta_g \sim \mathcal N(\mu, \sigma_\theta^2),\qquad \mu \sim \mathcal N(0, 10),\ \sigma_\theta \sim \text{HalfNormal}(1).\]

The joint posterior has \(G + 2\) parameters. Gibbs sampling exploits that \(\theta_g\) are conditionally independent given the hyperparameters, so we can update them in parallel.


A hybrid scheme updates the hyperparameters \((\mu, \sigma_\theta)\) from their conjugate Gaussian and half-Cauchy posteriors, and each \(\theta_g\) via a small Metropolis step conditional on \(\{y_{g1}, \ldots\}\) and the current hyperparameters. This is the Metropolis-within-Gibbs algorithm, which dominates practical Bayesian inference before HMC took over in the 2010s.


For small groups \(G\) with few observations each, hierarchical Bayes shrinks group estimates \(\theta_g\) toward the global mean \(\mu\) by exactly the same amount that James–Stein estimation does for a bank of Gaussians. This is one of the classical demonstrations that Bayes gives an operational meaning to shrinkage.
crumbs: 9  Gibbs sampling and high-dimensional inference

title: 9  Gibbs sampling and high-dimensional inference
text:
9.6 Modern developments
Since the 2010s the field has moved decisively toward Hamiltonian methods (HMC, NUTS) that scale better with dimension than either Metropolis or Gibbs. That said, Gibbs remains the algorithm of choice for models with discrete latent variables (mixtures, hidden Markov models, topic models like LDA), where Hamiltonian methods do not apply.
crumbs: 9  Gibbs sampling and high-dimensional inference

title: 9  Gibbs sampling and high-dimensional inference
text:
9.7 Exercises

For the basic Bernoulli-logistic model above, derive the Laplace approximation to the posterior and compare its standard deviation with a Metropolis estimate on simulated data.


Solution. The mode \(\hat\theta\) satisfies \(-\hat\theta/\tau^2 + n_1 - n\sigma(\hat\theta) = 0\), solvable numerically. The Hessian at the mode is \(-1/\tau^2 - n\sigma'(\hat\theta) = -1/\tau^2 - n\sigma(\hat\theta)(1 - \sigma(\hat\theta))\). Laplace: \(\pi(\theta \mid \mathbf y) \approx \mathcal N(\hat\theta,\ [-\text{Hess}]^{-1})\). Comparison to Metropolis with \(n = 200\): agreement within 1% for the standard deviation.


For a 2-component 1D Gaussian mixture with means at \(\pm 3\) and \(\sigma^2 = 1\), show that Gibbs sampling on the latent indicators mixes well when the empirical bimodal structure is clear but fails to escape local modes when components strongly overlap. What is the physical explanation?


Solution. Non-mixing between local modes of Gibbs is a label-switching / identifiability issue: the Gibbs chain rarely proposes swaps between clusters when the current assignments are all consistent, so the chain gets stuck in one labelling. Fixing requires either parallel tempering, reversible-jump MCMC, or symmetric priors that identify clusters by ordering (e.g. \(\mu_1 < \mu_2\)).
crumbs: 9  Gibbs sampling and high-dimensional inference

title: 9  Gibbs sampling and high-dimensional inference
text:
9.8 Callouts






Gibbs is simple and exact when conjugacy holds. When it doesn’t, either derive an auxiliary-variable augmentation (Pólya–Gamma, slice) or fall back to Metropolis-within-Gibbs.









Blocking correlated coordinates and updating them jointly (block Gibbs) dramatically improves mixing when strong correlations are present — the standard cure for slow mixing in hierarchical models.









Gibbs can catastrophically fail on multi-modal targets where individual conditionals are unimodal but the joint has multiple modes. Standard example: mixture models with symmetric priors.









The MCMC diagnostics of Chapter 7 (trace plots, ESS, \(\hat R\)) apply without change to Gibbs. Never trust a Gibbs chain without diagnostics — the fact that acceptance is 1 does not mean the chain has explored the target.

title: 10  A problem of high-dimensional inference
text:
10.1 9.1 Basic model
This chapter is a running example that ties Chapters 7–8 (MCMC, Gibbs) to a realistic Bayesian problem. It mirrors Prof. Allegra’s Chapter 11.
Suppose we observe \(n\) binary outcomes \(y_i \in \{0,1\}\) for \(i = 1, \ldots, n\), drawn as \(y_i \sim \text{Bern}(\sigma(\theta))\) where \(\sigma(z) = (1 + e^{-z})^{-1}\) is the logistic function. The parameter \(\theta\) has a Gaussian prior \(\theta \sim \mathcal N(0, \tau^2)\).
crumbs: 10  A problem of high-dimensional inference

title: 10  A problem of high-dimensional inference
text:
10.1.1 Likelihood and Metropolis approach
The unnormalised posterior is \[\pi(\theta \mid \mathbf y) \propto \exp\bigl(-\theta^2/(2\tau^2)\bigr)\prod_i \sigma(\theta)^{y_i}(1 - \sigma(\theta))^{1 - y_i}.\] There is no conjugate closed form. A Gaussian random-walk Metropolis proposal \(\theta' = \theta + \sigma_p\,\xi\) with \(\xi \sim \mathcal N(0,1)\) and standard acceptance ratio gives a working sampler.


10.1.2 Analytic form of the posterior
Even without conjugacy, the log-posterior admits a closed expression: \[\log \pi(\theta \mid \mathbf y) = -\frac{\theta^2}{2\tau^2} + n_1\,\theta - n\,\log(1 + e^\theta) + \text{const},\] with \(n_1 = \sum_i y_i\). The posterior is unimodal and concave, so a Laplace approximation around its mode gives a good analytic reference for benchmarking MCMC results.

Let \(\hat\theta = \arg\max_\theta \log\pi(\theta \mid \mathbf y)\) and \(J = -\partial^2_\theta \log\pi(\hat\theta \mid \mathbf y) > 0\). Then \(\pi(\theta \mid \mathbf y) \approx \mathcal N(\hat\theta, J^{-1})\) to leading order in \(n\). The mode \(\hat\theta\) solves \(-\hat\theta/\tau^2 + n_1 - n\sigma(\hat\theta) = 0\).



10.1.3 Simple numerical example

Simulate \(n = 200\) observations with true \(\theta = 0.5\) and prior \(\tau = 3\). Metropolis with \(\sigma_p = 0.3\) produces an acceptance rate \(\sim 40\%\) and an effective sample size of \(\sim 4000\) from \(10^4\) iterations. The posterior mean is close to \(0.5\) with standard deviation \(\sim 0.15\), agreeing with the Laplace approximation to 1%.



10.1.4 Gibbs sampling approach
For a scalar \(\theta\) there is nothing to Gibbs-decompose; the algorithm reduces to Metropolis. Gibbs becomes useful in the refined model below.
crumbs: 10  A problem of high-dimensional inference

title: 10  A problem of high-dimensional inference
text:
10.2 9.2 Refined model: hierarchical structure
Extend to \(G\) groups, each with its own signal \(\theta_g\): \[y_{gi} \sim \text{Bern}(\sigma(\theta_g)),\qquad \theta_g \sim \mathcal N(\mu, \sigma_\theta^2),\qquad \mu \sim \mathcal N(0, 10),\ \sigma_\theta \sim \text{HalfNormal}(1) .\] The joint posterior has \(G + 2\) parameters.

10.2.1 Metropolis-within-Gibbs

Alternate:

Update each \(\theta_g\) via a small Metropolis step conditional on \(\{y_{g1}, \ldots\}\) and the current \((\mu, \sigma_\theta)\).
Update \(\mu\) from its conjugate Gaussian posterior given \(\{\theta_g\}\).
Update \(\sigma_\theta\) from its (approximately conjugate) half-Cauchy posterior given \(\{\theta_g - \mu\}\).


This scheme was the dominant sampler for hierarchical Bayesian models before HMC/NUTS became standard.


10.2.2 Gibbs sampling
If we replaced the Bernoulli likelihood by a Gaussian one (e.g. \(y_{gi} \sim \mathcal N(\theta_g, \sigma_y^2)\)), full conjugacy would hold and pure Gibbs (no Metropolis) would sample the entire posterior in closed form. This is the classical example of hierarchical shrinkage — an analytical version of James–Stein estimation.

For small groups \(G\) with few observations each, hierarchical Bayes shrinks group estimates \(\theta_g\) toward the global mean \(\mu\) by exactly the same amount as James–Stein estimation. Bayes gives an operational meaning to shrinkage — via the hierarchical prior on \(\theta_g\).
crumbs: 10  A problem of high-dimensional inference

title: 10  A problem of high-dimensional inference
text:
10.3 Exercises

Derive the Laplace approximation of the basic-model posterior. Explain why it is an asymptotic approximation whose error tends to zero as \(n \to \infty\).


Solution. Compute \(\hat\theta\) numerically as the root of \(-\hat\theta/\tau^2 + n_1 - n\sigma(\hat\theta) = 0\); the second derivative is \(-1/\tau^2 - n\sigma(\hat\theta)(1 - \sigma(\hat\theta))\). As \(n \to \infty\) the posterior variance \(J^{-1} \to 0\) so the distribution concentrates at \(\hat\theta\); higher-order corrections to the Gaussian are \(O(1/n)\), formalised in the Bernstein–von Mises theorem.


Show that in the refined hierarchical model with Gaussian likelihood, the conditional distribution of \(\theta_g\) given the data and hyperparameters is Gaussian. Give its mean and variance.


Solution. \(\pi(\theta_g \mid \ldots) \propto \exp\bigl(-\tfrac{1}{2\sigma_y^2}\sum_{i}(y_{gi} - \theta_g)^2 - \tfrac{1}{2\sigma_\theta^2}(\theta_g - \mu)^2\bigr)\). Completing the square gives \[\theta_g \mid \ldots \sim \mathcal N\!\left(\frac{n_g \bar y_g / \sigma_y^2 + \mu / \sigma_\theta^2}{n_g/\sigma_y^2 + 1/\sigma_\theta^2},\ \left(n_g/\sigma_y^2 + 1/\sigma_\theta^2\right)^{-1}\right).\] The posterior mean is a precision-weighted average of the group sample mean and the hyperparameter mean — exactly the shrinkage interpretation.

title: 10  A problem of high-dimensional inference
text:
10.4 Callouts






The high-dimensional-inference chapter is a testing ground for the algorithms of Chapters 7 and 8. Every method (Metropolis, Gibbs, Metropolis-within-Gibbs) should be benchmarked against the Laplace reference before believing its output.









When designing a hierarchical model, always draw a plate diagram of the dependencies before writing code. Half of Bayesian bugs come from a mismatch between the intended model and its implementation.









Gibbs samplers for hierarchical models can mix very slowly when the variance hyperparameter \(\sigma_\theta\) is close to zero (a “funnel” geometry). Reparameterisation (non-centred, i.e. \(\theta_g = \mu + \sigma_\theta z_g\) with \(z_g \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)\)) is the standard fix.
