title: 11  Variational Bayes
text:
11.1 10.1 The variational principle
MCMC is asymptotically exact but slow. Variational Bayes (VB) trades exactness for speed: it approximates a posterior by the closest member of a tractable family, converting inference into optimisation. This chapter mirrors Prof. Allegra’s Chapter 12.
Given a target posterior \(p(\mathbf z \mid \mathbf x)\) we cannot compute directly, choose a tractable family \(\mathcal Q = \{q_\phi(\mathbf z)\}\) parameterised by \(\phi\), and find the member closest to \(p\) in KL divergence: \[\phi^* = \arg\min_\phi D\bigl(q_\phi(\mathbf z) \,\|\, p(\mathbf z \mid \mathbf x)\bigr) .\]
The ELBO decomposes as \(\mathcal L = \mathbb E_q[\log p(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf z)] - D(q_\phi(\mathbf z) \| p(\mathbf z))\) — a reconstruction fit minus a complexity penalty.

title: 11  Variational Bayes
text: The KL divergence \(D(q \| p)\) equals \(\log p(\mathbf x) - \mathcal L(\phi)\) where \[\mathcal L(\phi) = \mathbb E_{q_\phi}[\log p(\mathbf x, \mathbf z)] - \mathbb E_{q_\phi}[\log q_\phi(\mathbf z)]\] is the evidence lower bound. Since \(\log p(\mathbf x)\) does not depend on \(\phi\), maximising \(\mathcal L\) is equivalent to minimising the KL.

title: 11  Variational Bayes
text:
11.2 10.2 Mean-field approximation
The simplest tractable family assumes independence across coordinates:

The mean-field family on \(\mathbb R^d\) is \[q(\mathbf z) = \prod_{j=1}^{d} q_j(z_j) .\]

Under mean field, the optimal factor for coordinate \(j\) has an explicit form.

The mean-field ELBO is maximised by iterating \[q_j^*(z_j) \propto \exp\!\bigl(\mathbb E_{q_{-j}}[\log p(\mathbf x, \mathbf z)]\bigr),\] i.e. each factor’s log is the expected joint log-density under all other factors. This is coordinate ascent variational inference (CAVI) — the analogue of Gibbs sampling but with expectations replacing samples.

title: 11  Variational Bayes
text:
11.3 10.3 Example: one Gaussian

Model: \(x_i \sim \mathcal N(\mu, 1/\lambda)\) with priors \(\mu \sim \mathcal N(0, 1/\lambda_0)\), \(\lambda \sim \text{Gamma}(a_0, b_0)\). Mean-field factorisation \(q(\mu, \lambda) = q(\mu)q(\lambda)\):

\(q^*(\mu) = \mathcal N\bigl(m_n,\ 1/(\lambda_n + \lambda_0)\bigr)\) with \(\lambda_n = \mathbb E[\lambda] \cdot n\) and \(m_n\) a weighted mean.
\(q^*(\lambda) = \text{Gamma}(a_n, b_n)\) with \(a_n = a_0 + n/2\) and \(b_n\) a function of \(\mathbb E[(x_i - \mu)^2]\).

CAVI alternates between the two updates. Converges in \(\sim 10\) iterations to a solution that closely matches the exact NIG posterior.

title: 11  Variational Bayes
text:
11.4 10.4 Example: mixture distributions
For a \(K\)-component mixture model, mean-field VB introduces a variational cluster assignment \(q(z_i = k)\) and Gaussian variational distributions on each mean \(\mu_k\). The result is the variational EM algorithm — a Bayesian extension of standard EM that avoids over-fitting.

title: 11  Variational Bayes
text:
11.5 10.5 Variational autoencoders (VAE)
The most influential modern application of variational Bayes is the variational autoencoder (Kingma & Welling, 2014):

A VAE models data \(\mathbf x\) as generated by a latent code \(\mathbf z\) through a decoder network \(p_\theta(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf z)\) with \(\mathbf z \sim \mathcal N(0, I)\). The variational posterior is parameterised by an encoder network \(q_\phi(\mathbf z \mid \mathbf x) = \mathcal N(\boldsymbol\mu_\phi(\mathbf x),\ \boldsymbol\Sigma_\phi(\mathbf x))\). Training jointly optimises the ELBO w.r.t. \((\phi, \theta)\).

The reparameterisation trick \(\mathbf z = \boldsymbol\mu_\phi + \boldsymbol\Sigma_\phi^{1/2} \boldsymbol\epsilon\) with \(\boldsymbol\epsilon \sim \mathcal N(0, I)\) makes the ELBO differentiable through the sampling step, so stochastic gradients propagate cleanly through both networks.

Remark. VAEs revolutionised generative modelling: for the first time a single differentiable objective produced samples of natural images, speech, and molecules. Their descendants (β-VAE, VQ-VAE, hierarchical VAE) remain competitive with diffusion models for certain modalities.

title: 11  Variational Bayes
text:
11.6 Exercises

Derive the ELBO decomposition \(\mathcal L = \mathbb E_q[\log p(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf z)] - D(q \| p(\mathbf z))\).


Solution. \(\mathcal L = \mathbb E_q[\log p(\mathbf x, \mathbf z) - \log q(\mathbf z)] = \mathbb E_q[\log p(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf z) + \log p(\mathbf z) - \log q(\mathbf z)] = \mathbb E_q[\log p(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf z)] - D(q \| p(\mathbf z))\).


Show that mean-field VB underestimates posterior variance for correlated targets. Give a two-dimensional Gaussian example.


Solution. For a Gaussian target with covariance \(\Sigma\) and mean-field family \(q = \mathcal N(\boldsymbol\mu, \text{diag}(\boldsymbol\sigma^2))\), the optimal variance of \(q_j\) is \(1/(\Sigma^{-1})_{jj}\), which is less than \(\Sigma_{jj}\) whenever off-diagonal elements are non-zero. The intuition: mean field cannot capture correlations, so it compensates by inflating the “certainty” of each coordinate.

title: 11  Variational Bayes
text:
11.7 Callouts






Variational Bayes is biased by construction: the mean-field family cannot represent the true posterior in general. For applications where posterior shape matters (uncertainty quantification, decision theory), use HMC; for applications where posterior mean is enough (predictions, model comparison), VB is fine.









When implementing CAVI, initialise the variational parameters using a rough clustering of the data. Random initialisation often gets stuck in local ELBO maxima.









The mean-field variance under-estimation is a serious limitation for tasks like Bayesian neural networks where calibrated uncertainty is the whole point. Use normalising flows or low-rank variational families to escape it.

title: 12  Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
text:
12.1 11.1 Hamiltonian dynamics
Random-walk Metropolis (Chapter 7) mixes slowly in high dimensions. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) uses ideas from classical mechanics to propose distant, high-acceptance moves. This chapter mirrors Prof. Allegra’s Chapter 13.
Augment the state \(\mathbf q \in \mathbb R^d\) with an auxiliary momentum \(\mathbf p \in \mathbb R^d\), and define the Hamiltonian \[H(\mathbf q, \mathbf p) = U(\mathbf q) + K(\mathbf p) = -\log \pi(\mathbf q) + \tfrac12 \mathbf p^\top M^{-1}\mathbf p,\] where \(\pi\) is the target distribution, \(U = -\log\pi\) is the potential energy, and \(K\) is a Gaussian kinetic energy with mass matrix \(M\).

title: 12  Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
text: The Hamiltonian dynamics \[\dot{\mathbf q} = \partial_{\mathbf p} H = M^{-1}\mathbf p, \qquad \dot{\mathbf p} = -\partial_{\mathbf q} H = -\nabla U(\mathbf q)\] preserve the joint density \(e^{-H(\mathbf q, \mathbf p)}\) (Liouville’s theorem) and conserve energy (\(dH/dt = 0\)).

title: 12  Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
text:
12.2 11.2 Numerical integration: leapfrog
The continuous Hamiltonian flow cannot be integrated exactly. The leapfrog scheme is a symplectic integrator that preserves the volume of phase space and conserves \(H\) up to \(O(\Delta t^2)\) error:

Given step size \(\varepsilon\):

\(\mathbf p \leftarrow \mathbf p - \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\nabla U(\mathbf q)\) (half-step in momentum).
\(\mathbf q \leftarrow \mathbf q + \varepsilon M^{-1}\mathbf p\) (full step in position).
\(\mathbf p \leftarrow \mathbf p - \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\nabla U(\mathbf q)\) (half-step in momentum).


Composition of \(L\) leapfrog steps gives a proposal \((\mathbf q, \mathbf p) \to (\mathbf q', \mathbf p')\) with symplectic Jacobian equal to 1.

title: 12  Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
text:
12.3 11.3 The HMC algorithm

Given current \(\mathbf q\):

Sample momentum \(\mathbf p \sim \mathcal N(0, M)\).
Run \(L\) leapfrog steps of size \(\varepsilon\) starting from \((\mathbf q, \mathbf p)\), giving \((\mathbf q', \mathbf p')\).
Accept the proposal \(\mathbf q'\) with probability \[A = \min\bigl(1,\ \exp(H(\mathbf q, \mathbf p) - H(\mathbf q', \mathbf p'))\bigr) .\] Otherwise return \(\mathbf q\).


The acceptance probability depends only on the (small) integration error of the leapfrog scheme, not on the distance travelled. This is why HMC can propose moves of \(O(1)\) magnitude in high dimension while keeping acceptance \(\sim 0.7\).

Detailed balance holds: the HMC kernel leaves the joint distribution \(\pi(\mathbf q) \cdot \mathcal N(\mathbf p; 0, M)\) invariant. Consequently the marginal on \(\mathbf q\) is \(\pi\).

title: 12  Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
text:
12.4 11.4 Advantages of HMC
The essential reason HMC dominates in modern Bayesian inference is its dimension scaling:

For a target with sufficient regularity, the optimal number of leapfrog steps scales as \(L \sim d^{1/4}\) and the optimal step size as \(\varepsilon \sim d^{-1/4}\), giving an effective sample size per gradient evaluation of \(O(d^{-1/4})\). Random-walk Metropolis, by contrast, has ESS/eval \(\sim O(d^{-1})\).

The one-order-of-magnitude improvement in scaling is what made HMC the default sampler for continuous parameters.

Remark (NUTS). The No-U-Turn Sampler (Hoffman & Gelman, 2014) automates HMC by dynamically choosing \(L\) so the trajectory stops just before it starts curving back. NUTS is the algorithm underlying Stan, PyMC, and TensorFlow Probability.

title: 12  Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
text:
12.5 11.5 Practical considerations

12.5.1 Mass matrix
The mass matrix \(M\) acts as a preconditioner. For Gaussian-like targets, \(M = \text{diag}(\text{Var}(q_j)^{-1})\) or \(M = \Sigma_{\pi}^{-1}\) (the inverse target covariance) makes the Hamiltonian isotropic and improves mixing dramatically. Modern implementations estimate \(M\) from an initial warm-up phase.


12.5.2 Step size adaptation
If \(\varepsilon\) is too large the leapfrog error blows up and acceptance goes to zero; too small and \(L\) blows up. Dual averaging adapts \(\varepsilon\) during warm-up to hit a target acceptance \(\sim 0.8\).


12.5.3 Non-continuous targets
HMC requires a differentiable log-density. For discrete parameters or heavy-tailed distributions, HMC fails; Gibbs sampling or ensemble MCMC methods remain the tools of choice.

title: 12  Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
text:
12.6 Exercises

For a Gaussian target \(\pi(\mathbf q) = \mathcal N(0, \Sigma)\) show that Hamiltonian dynamics with \(M = \Sigma^{-1}\) decouples into independent harmonic oscillators along the eigenvectors of \(\Sigma\).


Solution. The Hamiltonian is \(H = \tfrac12 \mathbf q^\top \Sigma^{-1}\mathbf q + \tfrac12 \mathbf p^\top \Sigma\,\mathbf p\). Diagonalise \(\Sigma^{-1} = O \Lambda O^\top\) and transform \(\tilde{\mathbf q} = O^\top \mathbf q\), \(\tilde{\mathbf p} = O^\top \mathbf p\). Then \(H = \tfrac12 \tilde{\mathbf q}^\top \Lambda\,\tilde{\mathbf q} + \tfrac12 \tilde{\mathbf p}^\top \Lambda^{-1}\tilde{\mathbf p}\), a sum of independent harmonic oscillators. Each mode is analytically integrable — HMC is exact in this special case.


Show that the leapfrog integrator is reversible: swapping the sign of momentum and integrating backwards returns to the starting point.


Solution. Direct verification of the three-step definition: applying it with \(\varepsilon \to -\varepsilon\) inverts each step, and by symmetry of the composition the whole trajectory reverses exactly.

title: 12  Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
text:
12.7 Callouts






HMC is the modern MCMC sampler for continuous parameters. If your model is smooth and differentiable, use HMC/NUTS; use random-walk Metropolis only for discrete parameters or as a baseline.









When HMC has trouble mixing (low ESS, divergent transitions), reparameterise the model to make its geometry more isotropic. Non-centred parameterisations of hierarchical models are the canonical example.









The energy conservation of leapfrog holds up to \(O(\varepsilon^2)\) per step but without drift: energy oscillates but does not systematically increase. This is what makes long trajectories possible without a Metropolis correction blowing up.









HMC requires evaluating \(\nabla \log \pi(\mathbf q)\) at every leapfrog step. If your log-density is expensive (e.g. an ODE solve inside the likelihood), HMC can be prohibitively slow.

title: 13  Approximate Bayesian computation
text:
13.1 12.1 Motivation: intractable likelihoods
MCMC and VB all require the likelihood \(p(\mathbf y \mid \boldsymbol\theta)\) to be evaluable. What if the likelihood is only simulable — i.e. we can generate data from the model but cannot compute its density? That is the world of approximate Bayesian computation (ABC). This chapter mirrors Prof. Allegra’s Chapter 14.
Many scientific models are defined by a simulator: a stochastic dynamical system that emits synthetic data given parameters. The associated likelihood may be:
For such models MCMC’s Metropolis acceptance ratio \(\pi(\theta')/\pi(\theta)\) cannot be computed. ABC solves this by working directly with simulations.

title: 13  Approximate Bayesian computation
text:
an intractable marginal (e.g. a hidden-state model where the joint is tractable but the observed marginal is not),
an unnormalised density with an intractable partition function (e.g. certain physics-inspired models),
entirely implicit (e.g. agent-based simulations in ecology and epidemiology).

title: 13  Approximate Bayesian computation
text:
13.2 12.2 ABC rejection sampling

Given observed data \(\mathbf y_{obs}\), prior \(\pi(\theta)\), simulator \(S(\theta)\), distance \(d(\cdot, \cdot)\), and tolerance \(\epsilon\):
Repeat until \(N\) samples are accepted:

Draw \(\theta^{(i)} \sim \pi(\theta)\).
Simulate \(\mathbf y^{(i)} = S(\theta^{(i)})\).
If \(d(\mathbf y^{(i)}, \mathbf y_{obs}) < \epsilon\), accept \(\theta^{(i)}\).


The accepted samples are distributed as \(\pi_\epsilon(\theta \mid \mathbf y_{obs})\), which converges to \(\pi(\theta \mid \mathbf y_{obs})\) as \(\epsilon \to 0\).

Remark. ABC replaces the (unavailable) likelihood ratio by an indicator on distance — a very general trick. Its downside is that acceptance is \(\ll 1\) when \(\epsilon\) is small, so ABC-rejection is impractical for anything but toy problems.

title: 13  Approximate Bayesian computation
text:
13.3 12.3 ABC-MCMC and ABC-SMC
Two improvements make ABC practical:

Combine ABC with a Metropolis proposal on \(\theta\): propose \(\theta' \sim q(\theta' \mid \theta)\), simulate \(\mathbf y'\), and accept with probability \[A = \min\!\left(1,\ \frac{\pi(\theta')\,q(\theta \mid \theta')}{\pi(\theta)\,q(\theta' \mid \theta)}\right)\cdot \mathbf 1[d(\mathbf y', \mathbf y_{obs}) < \epsilon] .\] The chain concentrates on regions of the parameter space where simulations resemble the data.


Sequential Monte Carlo variant: start with \(\epsilon_1\) large and gradually anneal \(\epsilon_t \searrow \epsilon_{final}\), reweighting particles as \(\epsilon\) shrinks. Widely used in population genetics and epidemiology.

title: 13  Approximate Bayesian computation
text:
13.4 12.4 Summary statistics
For high-dimensional data \(\mathbf y\), the raw distance \(d(\mathbf y', \mathbf y_{obs})\) is nearly always huge; ABC becomes uninformative. The standard remedy is to summarise \(\mathbf y\) by a low-dimensional statistic \(T(\mathbf y)\) and require \(d(T(\mathbf y'), T(\mathbf y_{obs})) < \epsilon\).

If \(T\) is a sufficient statistic for \(\theta\), ABC on \(T\) has the same posterior as ABC on the raw data, i.e. no information is lost. In practice sufficient statistics rarely exist; carefully-chosen summary statistics (empirical moments, quantiles, autocorrelations) are used instead.


Remark (Learned summary statistics). Modern ABC uses neural networks to learn near-sufficient summary statistics automatically. Neural posterior estimation (Papamakarios & Murray, 2016) trains a conditional density \(q_\phi(\theta \mid T(\mathbf y))\) to match the true posterior, blending ABC with variational Bayes.

title: 13  Approximate Bayesian computation
text:
13.5 12.5 Applications

The coalescent model produces gene genealogies whose likelihood is intractable but easily simulable. ABC is the standard tool for inferring demographic parameters (population size, migration rates, split times) from DNA data. Beaumont et al. (2002) is the seminal reference.


Agent-based models of infectious-disease spread are intractable but simulable. ABC-SMC was used during COVID-19 to fit parameters of the UK’s SPI-M models given hospitalisation time series.

title: 13  Approximate Bayesian computation
text:
13.6 Exercises

Show that ABC rejection with \(\epsilon = 0\) (and continuous data) has acceptance probability zero.


Solution. For continuous \(\mathbf y\), \(P(\mathbf y' = \mathbf y_{obs}) = 0\). The Dirac-delta indicator is never triggered. Hence any positive tolerance \(\epsilon > 0\) is a necessary approximation for continuous data.


For a Gaussian likelihood \(\mathbf y \mid \theta \sim \mathcal N(\theta, I)\) with a Gaussian prior, show that ABC with sufficient statistic \(T = \bar y\) recovers the exact posterior in the limit \(\epsilon \to 0\).


Solution. \(\bar y\) is a sufficient statistic for \(\theta\). As \(\epsilon \to 0\) the ABC posterior converges to the true posterior conditional on \(\bar y = \bar y_{obs}\), which by sufficiency equals the true posterior conditional on the full data.

title: 13  Approximate Bayesian computation
text:
13.7 Callouts






ABC is the tool for likelihood-free inference. Every scientific problem where a simulator is the model’s definition (not a computational shortcut) is a candidate.









When designing an ABC study, invest time in choosing summary statistics. The success of ABC hinges on their sufficiency; a bad choice makes the posterior arbitrarily far from the truth.









ABC posteriors are biased estimators of the true posterior. Studies that report ABC results should always report the tolerance \(\epsilon\) and, ideally, a robustness check as \(\epsilon\) is decreased.









Simulation-based inference (SBI), including modern neural variants, has largely superseded classical ABC for high-dimensional problems. Consult the sbi Python library for state-of-the-art tools.
